## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and the starting architecture scores 0.000 on both seeds. The default recipe gives only 131,072 steps in batches of 256×16, so that is just 32 PPO updates. That is very few policy-improvement steps for a task that needs many correct placements in a row, and the recipe may be the main bottleneck. Networks cheaper than the starting one get no extra steps (r is floored at 1), so the FLOPs up to r≈1 are effectively free. This round splits the question: (1) the same network with smaller batches and fewer epochs, giving about 118 updates; (2) the same network with 1 epoch and 64 envs, giving about 416 updates; (3) a new network built per layer at about the same cost, on recipe (1). It should make it easier to learn the landing layer (max height under the footprint) and whether a brick fits exactly at that layer. Comparing (1) with (3) isolates the architecture; comparing (1) with (2) maps the recipe.

### Round 2
Every trial so far scores 0 on dev and 0 on training success, so nothing yet separates the candidates and seed noise cannot be judged. Changing only the recipe (1, 2 or 4 epochs) left the baseline at 0. The per-layer logsumexp net was very small (W=24, HID=16) and also scored 0. To place a brick safely, the agent must compare the landing layer L (the highest build cell under the footprint) with each cell's next missing target layer. The baseline head sees only max, min and mean of a linear projection over the footprint, which may make that comparison hard to learn. This round makes larger changes to the network: (A) a head that runs a full MLP over the brick's footprint window; (A′) the same network with a long-horizon recipe, since the +1 exact-build bonus may be discounted away; (B) a head that learns a distribution over each column's height and uses it to weight per-layer scores.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and none built a single design exactly even during training. That held across five recipes (1–2 epochs, 32–416 updates, gamma 0.95 or 0.99) and four head designs. All four heads share one assumption: logits are produced per cell, with brick type as the outer index and the anchor at the top-left. The task warns that this world may not behave as described. If the action indexing or anchor rule is different (type as the inner index, x and y swapped, or a different anchor), every per-cell head would point features at the wrong actions. That could explain a flat zero no matter the recipe. The most useful test now is a head that makes no assumption about the action layout: dense (fully connected) heads and learned per-action attention queries. If any of these goes above 0, the action layout is the bottleneck.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0, on dev and on training success. That covers different heads (pooled, footprint-window, per-layer, dense, attention), different recipes and different horizons. Because the network made no difference, I suspect one cause affects every trial. My best guess is that the policy collapses to calling DONE. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so their reward is negative (about -0.09 per step), while DONE gives 0. The DONE logit gains early, episodes get short, and the agent rarely samples the good placements it needs to learn from. Normalised advantages and an entropy coefficient of 0.01 do little to stop this. I could not observe this directly; it is an inference. The last round tests remedies for this collapse: a high entropy bonus, a longer discount horizon so that future positive placements outweigh stopping, and a DONE logit that learns more slowly. Two use the cheap baseline network and one uses the window head, which had the most detailed per-placement view of the cells.
